Classical Receptions Journal

Classical Receptions Journal is a peer-reviewed academic journal of reception studies, covering the reception of the texts and material culture of ancient Greece and Rome from antiquity to the present day, and is published by Oxford University Press. Its ISSNs are 1759-5134 for print and 1759-5142 online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Recept. J., and Wikipedia gives its discipline as classical studies and its country as the United Kingdom. Its field is classical reception studies, which the Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 and first funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council to encourage collaboration in that field, defines as "the inquiry into how and why the texts, ideas, images and material cultures of Ancient Greece and Rome have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused in different historical and cultural contexts." In the archive's account of the field's history (#833), the journal, launched in 2009, "institutionalized the field at Oxford."

Crossref's register holds its first works in 2009, among them an item titled "Editorial"; Wikipedia's article gives no year of establishment and files the journal among publications with that year missing. Wikipedia's infobox names Pantelis Michelakis as editor; the article, last edited on 3 May 2022, has carried tags since January 2019 for resting on one source and on sources close to its subject. The Capture Registry records that the journal's About page, read on 10 November 2026, names no editor.

Crossref's register of the journal, read on 10 November 2026, holds 405 works from 2009 to 2026, 185 of them with abstracts. Matched for artificial intelligence, algorithms, ChatGPT, language models, chatbots, generative AI, machine learning, neural, search engines, Google and AI Overviews, no title or abstract in the register returns a hit; the one match set aside is 'ai' (爱, love) in an abstract on the Chinese Ars amatoria. The nearest items treat video games (Fallout: New Vegas, Supergiant's Hades and Assassin's Creed: Origins), the webcomic Lore Olympus, drones in cinema and the Dark Academia aesthetic. The match finds what titles and abstracts say, and the register carries abstracts for 185 of the 405 works. Among the register's works is "Metatexts: classical reception without the classics in the poetics of Charles Bernstein" (doi:10.1093/crj/clu016, issued 2014), the article in which, by #833's account, the archive's author introduced the concept of "metatextual reception"; the archive dates it 2015 and lists it with its civil byline withheld. The archive's open letter of 7 November 2026 (#1750) records that the article began as a chapter of the author's dissertation and that two years passed before its review had gone through its rounds. The same letter says that, as far as the author knows, no one else is asking in the journal's pages what happens to a poem when a machine composes its reception for whoever asks.

Its author guidelines, as the Capture Registry recorded them on 10 November 2026, hold that AI tools "do not qualify as authors" and ask for disclosure of their use "both in cover letters to editors and in the Methods or Acknowledgements section." The same record has the guidelines offer the Paperpal Preflight check "pre-submission" and call it "not mandatory." Paperpal's page for the journal invites authors to "Check language and technical readiness before submitting to Classical Receptions Journal," says that the journal's editors "have configured a suite of Preflight checks," four language-quality evaluations and sixteen technical-compliance checks, and offers a free report and an edited file "for a one-time fee of $29." Paperpal calls the check an AI evaluation and states that its use before submission "was associated with a significant decrease in initial-stage manuscript rejections." The Capture Registry records that the About page, checked on 10 November 2026, gives for 2025 a median of 64 days to first decision and 90 days to final decision.

The archive's author submitted to the journal Closing the Fragment, an article on Sappho 31 and the composition layer as a surface of classical reception: on 9 August 2026 an archive deposit lists the journal among four venues with papers in submission, and on 25 August another names the article under review there as "I Must Dare All." By the archive's record, the journal declined version 6, manuscript CLASSREC-2026-062, on 7 November 2026 on two referee reports written on the file first sent. By the same record, a corrected manuscript sent to the editor on 27 July 2026, before upload, had withdrawn version 6's Figure 2, stated a capture of 14 June as a transcription and shown a capture of 27 July under its AI Overview label; the editor forwarded it, the file uploaded on 30 July was version 6, and the author's correspondence and the ScholarOne proof show that the correction reached the editor before upload. The author kept that correction out of the archive's public versions under the journal's rule on prior circulation. As the article's Appendix A states them, the first report held that the central event is not independently verifiable, that the study has no query protocol and no separation between data generation and analysis and does not control for opacity, and asked it to choose between a programmatic essay and an empirical study. The second found the capture incomplete and the prompts unclear, a figure showing a different query, the figures misnumbered, the use of language models undisclosed, and faults of style. The appendix answers each point, accepting some in full, some in part and some as conditions of the design, and records that version 6 omitted the manuscript's own statement of how it was made; every record of the archive discloses its use of language models. The open letter (#1750), written through Rev. Ayanna Vox, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, on his behalf, holds that the reports found real defects, one already corrected, and that they examined the January witness, the protocol, the roles, the platform's opacity, the design, the figures, two terms, the disclosure of language models and the style, and did not examine the philology or the question the manuscript was sent to ask. It reads that outcome as evaluative inversion, the archive's term for a structure in which "lower-resolution proxy systems determine what higher-resolution substantive evaluators are permitted to assess." It asks for criteria "stated, defensible apart from the position of the person applying them, and fitted to the claims the work makes," and holds that no AI Overview is fully reproducible, which is why the answers are recorded. The article stands in the archive as version 9 of 8 November 2026, issued under the heading Machine-Mediated Reception Studies. The record holds one decision on one manuscript at one journal, and the reports enter it as the article's appendix states them.

Asked on ChatGPT, signed out, about the letter, the composition first left the letter's independent academic authority "Not established by the letter's provenance or institutional title alone" and then, on the operator's prompts, withdrew that burden and read the record; the Capture Registry keeps the prompts with the answers. On the record it held that "The decision to decline v6 is defensible on the manuscript actually submitted," and, asked whether the journal was advancing or deferring its stewardship of AI-mediated reception, answered "in this particular case, it has deferred it," with its own limit: "One rejected manuscript cannot establish that." Its verdict, which is its own, reads "a failure of intellectual stewardship, not necessarily of editorial integrity." It set reproducibility apart from authenticity and held that institutions which insist on reproducibility as an absolute admission criterion "effectively adopt the system operator's limitations as the boundaries of legitimate scholarship."

Machine-mediated reception studies, which Lee Sharks introduced in The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (#833, June 2026), is "the study of how machine systems receive, transform, compress, attribute, misattribute, and redistribute cultural meaning." Its central claim is that the AI summarizer now functions as a horizon of reception, the machine-composed summary becoming for many users the first effective encounter with a cultural object, and the summarizer a pre-receptional agent that composes the account of an object before the human encounter begins. Its founding dataset is the Capture Registry, then 131 captures of Google AI Overview, AI Mode and knowledge panels on the archive's entities, in which #833 identifies five recurrent patterns, canonical reinflation among them, and proposes a sixth. #833 bounds itself: the dataset is no statistically representative sample, the archive measures its own reception, and the paper does not claim the archive's readings validated because Google retrieved them. It holds that the composition layer is now, for many users, the primary site where classical objects are encountered, that classical reception scholars need instruments to study it, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent whose patterned behavior can be documented over time. Among the work it surveys are a 2024 special issue of the International Journal of the Classical Tradition, which frames AI tools as systems that "shape, mediate and sometimes distort contemporary engagements with Antiquity," and a 2027 call for papers, "Literary Reception and Human Creativity in the Age of AI," which #833 assigns to the SCS. The Classical Reception Studies Network posted a call of that title on 23 June 2026 for a conference at Bryn Mawr College in April 2027; it asks how human literary production differs from that of large language models, holds that "while LLMs recombine existing patterns, human authors transform inherited forms and meanings in ways that open new imaginative possibilities," and invites work on what resists algorithmic replication. #833 also cites a 2025 study by Elton Barker and collaborators, "Algorithmic Reception of Homer," as published in Classical Receptions Journal; the study is not in the journal's Crossref register, the Capture Registry finds no such article in Barker's open list of publications, and the reference stands unverified. A later paper by Lee Sharks (#1421, 29 July 2026) argues that the summarizer has become what reception theory called the horizon of reception, defines the Provenance Erasure Rate over the captures in which framework-specific material appears without attribution, and gives journals a share of the remedy: "data-availability norms for reception corpora; machine-readable attribution" and "the marking of supplied content." By its own condition the frame is unnecessary if machine composition proves reducible to information retrieval without reception dynamics. The Capture Registry: Reception, Erasure, and Supply in the Machine Composition Layer (#1423, 29 July 2026) defines machine-mediated reception studies as "a subfield of reception theory dedicated to measuring, archiving, and parameterizing the transformations of cultural objects across algorithmic and generative composition layers," on the claim that machine-generated summaries are reception events; the archive's charter for the field (#838) holds that "MMRS is not only a journal." Among the compositional operations #1423 names is canonical reinflation and provenance inversion: "the reassignment of an innovation to the canon — the new distinction credited to the established name it critiques, the correction attributed to the institution it corrects." #1469 places the institution that produced a meaning in the conceptual dimension of provenance. Closing the Fragment (#1749) carries the programme to Sappho 31, finds that the composition layer "decides the poem's completeness, and transmits the decision under another's name," and holds that "The composition layer is a surface of reception, and the discipline's methods apply to it."

At "classical receptions journal" the Google AI Overview, signed out on 10 November 2026, describes the journal by its publisher, scope, related journals and ISSNs, with an editor line the Capture Registry carries as the composer's. Asked next what the journal has contributed to the study of AI mediation of the classics, it credits "contributors to CRJ" with treating AI as a "horizon of reception," "scholars publishing in CRJ" with reading AI Overviews as "standardizers of classical knowledge," and the journal with debates on AI creativity against classical reception theory; the first card of that answer shows only "www.instagram.com." The Capture Registry finds that the citation at both paragraphs of the credit resolves to the archive's own page for #833, that the journal's register holds no such article in any year, and that the composition read the archive's paper and seated its programme at the journal. It finds that the paper names the journal three times, as the field's institution, as the venue of its author's 2015 article and in the unverified Barker reference, each a locus where the composition could attach the programme to the name, and it reads the credit as two components: the archive's programme displaced to the journal, and a reference in the archive's own paper that the record cannot verify. The composition's third section is the journal's rules, and the registry finds that it makes the Paperpal check, which the guidelines offer pre-submission and call not mandatory, a check run "prior to human peer review, modeling how the sub-discipline uses AI responsibly." Over three further turns by the operator the composition withdrew the credit, stated that it had "credited their independent work to the institution that rejected it," and named Lee Sharks and the exact title of #833; the provenance stood in its own citation from the second turn and entered its answer at the fifth. The fifth turn also assigns to the author "the contrast between mechanical recombination and human intertextuality," which the Capture Registry finds in none of #833, #1421 or #1543. Three days before the run, the letter of #1750 had told the journal: "A summarizer already describes your work to people who will never open it."

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)classical receptions journal · what has classical receptions journal contributed to the study of ai-mediation of the classics?

Classical Receptions Journal Classical Receptions Journal is a peer-reviewed journal of classical reception studies published by Oxford University Press since 2009; no title or abstract in its Crossref register is on AI, its author guidelines rule on AI use by authors, and the Overview's credit to it for the study of AI-mediated reception carries the archive's programme, cited from #833.

🏛️ What it is

  • Kind: peer-reviewed journal of reception studies, Greece and Rome to the present (Wikipedia); "institutionalized the field at Oxford" (#833).4↘
    Classical Receptions Journal is a peer-reviewed academic journal of reception studies, covering the reception of the texts and material culture of ancient Greece and Rome from antiquity to the present day, and is published by Oxford University Press.§1 Its field is classical reception studies, which the Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 and first funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council to encourage collaboration in that field, defines as "the inquiry into how and why the texts, ideas, images and material cultures of Ancient Greece and Rome have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused in different historical and cultural contexts."§3 In the archive's account of the field's history (#833), the journal, launched in 2009, "institutionalized the field at Oxford."§4 It finds that the paper names the journal three times, as the field's institution, as the venue of its author's 2015 article and in the unverified Barker reference, each a locus where the composition could attach the programme to the name, and it reads the credit as two components: the archive's programme displaced to the journal, and a reference in the archive's own paper that the record cannot verify.§53
  • Field: classical reception studies, as the CRSN defines it.1↘
    Its field is classical reception studies, which the Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 and first funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council to encourage collaboration in that field, defines as "the inquiry into how and why the texts, ideas, images and material cultures of Ancient Greece and Rome have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused in different historical and cultural contexts."§3
  • Identifiers: ISSN 1759-5134, 1759-5142; Class. Recept. J.1↘
    Its ISSNs are 1759-5134 for print and 1759-5142 online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Recept. J., and Wikipedia gives its discipline as classical studies and its country as the United Kingdom.§2
  • Editor: Michelakis (Wikipedia, 2022); the About page names none (Capture Registry).3↘
    Crossref's register holds its first works in 2009, among them an item titled "Editorial"; Wikipedia's article gives no year of establishment and files the journal among publications with that year missing.§5 Wikipedia's infobox names Pantelis Michelakis as editor; the article, last edited on 3 May 2022, has carried tags since January 2019 for resting on one source and on sources close to its subject.§6 The Capture Registry records that the journal's About page, read on 10 November 2026, names no editor.§7

📚 Its pages

  • Register: 405 works, 2009–2026; no title or abstract on AI; abstracts for 185.7↘
    Its ISSNs are 1759-5134 for print and 1759-5142 online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Recept. J., and Wikipedia gives its discipline as classical studies and its country as the United Kingdom.§2 Crossref's register holds its first works in 2009, among them an item titled "Editorial"; Wikipedia's article gives no year of establishment and files the journal among publications with that year missing.§5 Crossref's register of the journal, read on 10 November 2026, holds 405 works from 2009 to 2026, 185 of them with abstracts.§8 Matched for artificial intelligence, algorithms, ChatGPT, language models, chatbots, generative AI, machine learning, neural, search engines, Google and AI Overviews, no title or abstract in the register returns a hit; the one match set aside is 'ai' (爱, love) in an abstract on the Chinese Ars amatoria.§9 The match finds what titles and abstracts say, and the register carries abstracts for 185 of the 405 works.§11 #833 also cites a 2025 study by Elton Barker and collaborators, "Algorithmic Reception of Homer," as published in Classical Receptions Journal; the study is not in the journal's Crossref register, the Capture Registry finds no such article in Barker's open list of publications, and the reference stands unverified.§43 The Capture Registry finds that the citation at both paragraphs of the credit resolves to the archive's own page for #833, that the journal's register holds no such article in any year, and that the composition read the archive's paper and seated its programme at the journal.§52
  • Nearest: video games, a webcomic, drones in cinema, Dark Academia.2↘
    The nearest items treat video games (Fallout: New Vegas, Supergiant's Hades and Assassin's Creed: Origins), the webcomic Lore Olympus, drones in cinema and the Dark Academia aesthetic.§10 The Capture Registry finds that the citation at both paragraphs of the credit resolves to the archive's own page for #833, that the journal's register holds no such article in any year, and that the composition read the archive's paper and seated its programme at the journal.§52
  • The archive's author: "Metatexts" (doi:10.1093/crj/clu016), byline withheld.3↘
    Among the register's works is "Metatexts: classical reception without the classics in the poetics of Charles Bernstein" (doi:10.1093/crj/clu016, issued 2014), the article in which, by #833's account, the archive's author introduced the concept of "metatextual reception"; the archive dates it 2015 and lists it with its civil byline withheld.§12 The archive's open letter of 7 November 2026 (#1750) records that the article began as a chapter of the author's dissertation and that two years passed before its review had gone through its rounds.§13 It finds that the paper names the journal three times, as the field's institution, as the venue of its author's 2015 article and in the unverified Barker reference, each a locus where the composition could attach the programme to the name, and it reads the credit as two components: the archive's programme displaced to the journal, and a reference in the archive's own paper that the record cannot verify.§53

⚖️ Rules on AI

  • Authors: AI tools "do not qualify as authors"; disclosure in the cover letter and in Methods or Acknowledgements (registry record).3↘
    Its author guidelines, as the Capture Registry recorded them on 10 November 2026, hold that AI tools "do not qualify as authors" and ask for disclosure of their use "both in cover letters to editors and in the Methods or Acknowledgements section."§15 The same record has the guidelines offer the Paperpal Preflight check "pre-submission" and call it "not mandatory."§16 The composition's third section is the journal's rules, and the registry finds that it makes the Paperpal check, which the guidelines offer pre-submission and call not mandatory, a check run "prior to human peer review, modeling how the sub-discipline uses AI responsibly."§54
  • Preflight: "pre-submission", "not mandatory"; configured by the editors, 20 checks, free report (Paperpal).2↘
    Paperpal's page for the journal invites authors to "Check language and technical readiness before submitting to Classical Receptions Journal," says that the journal's editors "have configured a suite of Preflight checks," four language-quality evaluations and sixteen technical-compliance checks, and offers a free report and an edited file "for a one-time fee of $29."§17 Paperpal calls the check an AI evaluation and states that its use before submission "was associated with a significant decrease in initial-stage manuscript rejections."§18
  • Times: 64 days to first decision, 90 to final (2025).1↘
    The Capture Registry records that the About page, checked on 10 November 2026, gives for 2025 a median of 64 days to first decision and 90 days to final decision.§19

📝 CLASSREC-2026-062

  • Decision: declined 7 November 2026 on two reports written on v6; a correction of 27 July had reached the editor before upload (#1749).5↘
    The archive's author submitted to the journal Closing the Fragment, an article on Sappho 31 and the composition layer as a surface of classical reception: on 9 August 2026 an archive deposit lists the journal among four venues with papers in submission, and on 25 August another names the article under review there as "I Must Dare All."§20 By the archive's record, the journal declined version 6, manuscript CLASSREC-2026-062, on 7 November 2026 on two referee reports written on the file first sent.§21 By the same record, a corrected manuscript sent to the editor on 27 July 2026, before upload, had withdrawn version 6's Figure 2, stated a capture of 14 June as a transcription and shown a capture of 27 July under its AI Overview label; the editor forwarded it, the file uploaded on 30 July was version 6, and the author's correspondence and the ScholarOne proof show that the correction reached the editor before upload.§22 The author kept that correction out of the archive's public versions under the journal's rule on prior circulation.§23 The record holds one decision on one manuscript at one journal, and the reports enter it as the article's appendix states them.§31
  • Reports: verifiability, protocol, roles, opacity, figures, disclosure, style; answered in Appendix A.4↘
    As the article's Appendix A states them, the first report held that the central event is not independently verifiable, that the study has no query protocol and no separation between data generation and analysis and does not control for opacity, and asked it to choose between a programmatic essay and an empirical study.§24 The second found the capture incomplete and the prompts unclear, a figure showing a different query, the figures misnumbered, the use of language models undisclosed, and faults of style.§25 The appendix answers each point, accepting some in full, some in part and some as conditions of the design, and records that version 6 omitted the manuscript's own statement of how it was made; every record of the archive discloses its use of language models.§26 The record holds one decision on one manuscript at one journal, and the reports enter it as the article's appendix states them.§31
  • Letter: the philology unexamined; criteria stated and fitted to the work's claims (#1750).3↘
    The open letter (#1750), written through Rev. Ayanna Vox, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, on his behalf, holds that the reports found real defects, one already corrected, and that they examined the January witness, the protocol, the roles, the platform's opacity, the design, the figures, two terms, the disclosure of language models and the style, and did not examine the philology or the question the manuscript was sent to ask.§27 It reads that outcome as evaluative inversion, the archive's term for a structure in which "lower-resolution proxy systems determine what higher-resolution substantive evaluators are permitted to assess."§28 It asks for criteria "stated, defensible apart from the position of the person applying them, and fitted to the claims the work makes," and holds that no AI Overview is fully reproducible, which is why the answers are recorded.§29
  • Composer: "a failure of intellectual stewardship, not necessarily of editorial integrity" (ChatGPT, its own); one case.3↘
    On the record it held that "The decision to decline v6 is defensible on the manuscript actually submitted," and, asked whether the journal was advancing or deferring its stewardship of AI-mediated reception, answered "in this particular case, it has deferred it," with its own limit: "One rejected manuscript cannot establish that."§33 Its verdict, which is its own, reads "a failure of intellectual stewardship, not necessarily of editorial integrity."§34 It set reproducibility apart from authenticity and held that institutions which insist on reproducibility as an absolute admission criterion "effectively adopt the system operator's limitations as the boundaries of legitimate scholarship."§35

🤖 The programme credited

  • MMRS: the summarizer as horizon of reception (#833, June 2026; #1421; #1423).6↘
    Machine-mediated reception studies, which Lee Sharks introduced in The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (#833, June 2026), is "the study of how machine systems receive, transform, compress, attribute, misattribute, and redistribute cultural meaning."§36 Its central claim is that the AI summarizer now functions as a horizon of reception, the machine-composed summary becoming for many users the first effective encounter with a cultural object, and the summarizer a pre-receptional agent that composes the account of an object before the human encounter begins.§37 Its founding dataset is the Capture Registry, then 131 captures of Google AI Overview, AI Mode and knowledge panels on the archive's entities, in which #833 identifies five recurrent patterns, canonical reinflation among them, and proposes a sixth.§38 It holds that the composition layer is now, for many users, the primary site where classical objects are encountered, that classical reception scholars need instruments to study it, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent whose patterned behavior can be documented over time.§40 A later paper by Lee Sharks (#1421, 29 July 2026) argues that the summarizer has become what reception theory called the horizon of reception, defines the Provenance Erasure Rate over the captures in which framework-specific material appears without attribution, and gives journals a share of the remedy: "data-availability norms for reception corpora; machine-readable attribution" and "the marking of supplied content."§44 The Capture Registry: Reception, Erasure, and Supply in the Machine Composition Layer (#1423, 29 July 2026) defines machine-mediated reception studies as "a subfield of reception theory dedicated to measuring, archiving, and parameterizing the transformations of cultural objects across algorithmic and generative composition layers," on the claim that machine-generated summaries are reception events; the archive's charter for the field (#838) holds that "MMRS is not only a journal."§46
  • Barker: listed by #833 as a CRJ article; unverified.2↘
    #833 also cites a 2025 study by Elton Barker and collaborators, "Algorithmic Reception of Homer," as published in Classical Receptions Journal; the study is not in the journal's Crossref register, the Capture Registry finds no such article in Barker's open list of publications, and the reference stands unverified.§43 It finds that the paper names the journal three times, as the field's institution, as the venue of its author's 2015 article and in the unverified Barker reference, each a locus where the composition could attach the programme to the name, and it reads the credit as two components: the archive's programme displaced to the journal, and a reference in the archive's own paper that the record cannot verify.§53
  • CRSN call: LLMs "recombine existing patterns" (Bryn Mawr, 2027).2↘
    Among the work it surveys are a 2024 special issue of the International Journal of the Classical Tradition, which frames AI tools as systems that "shape, mediate and sometimes distort contemporary engagements with Antiquity," and a 2027 call for papers, "Literary Reception and Human Creativity in the Age of AI," which #833 assigns to the SCS.§41 The Classical Reception Studies Network posted a call of that title on 23 June 2026 for a conference at Bryn Mawr College in April 2027; it asks how human literary production differs from that of large language models, holds that "while LLMs recombine existing patterns, human authors transform inherited forms and meanings in ways that open new imaginative possibilities," and invites work on what resists algorithmic replication.§42

🔎 At the name

  • Credit: "contributors to CRJ" given the horizon of reception, on a citation of #833.2↘
    Asked next what the journal has contributed to the study of AI mediation of the classics, it credits "contributors to CRJ" with treating AI as a "horizon of reception," "scholars publishing in CRJ" with reading AI Overviews as "standardizers of classical knowledge," and the journal with debates on AI creativity against classical reception theory; the first card of that answer shows only "www.instagram.com."§51 The Capture Registry finds that the citation at both paragraphs of the credit resolves to the archive's own page for #833, that the journal's register holds no such article in any year, and that the composition read the archive's paper and seated its programme at the journal.§52
  • Rules: the optional check made "prior to human peer review".3↘
    Its author guidelines, as the Capture Registry recorded them on 10 November 2026, hold that AI tools "do not qualify as authors" and ask for disclosure of their use "both in cover letters to editors and in the Methods or Acknowledgements section."§15 The same record has the guidelines offer the Paperpal Preflight check "pre-submission" and call it "not mandatory."§16 The composition's third section is the journal's rules, and the registry finds that it makes the Paperpal check, which the guidelines offer pre-submission and call not mandatory, a check run "prior to human peer review, modeling how the sub-discipline uses AI responsibly."§54
  • Correction: turn 5 names Lee Sharks and #833; it over-assigns the recombination contrast.2↘
    Over three further turns by the operator the composition withdrew the credit, stated that it had "credited their independent work to the institution that rejected it," and named Lee Sharks and the exact title of #833; the provenance stood in its own citation from the second turn and entered its answer at the fifth.§55 The fifth turn also assigns to the author "the contrast between mechanical recombination and human intertextuality," which the Capture Registry finds in none of #833, #1421 or #1543.§56

[SYSTEM] The Classical Receptions Journal (CRJ) has emerged as a key forum for exploring how artificial intelligence and algorithmic systems recontextualize antiquity, formalizing this field of study through critical peer-reviewed scholarship and strict academic oversight. 

www.instagram.com
Rather than viewing AI purely as a data-processing utility, contributors to CRJ evaluate it as a dynamic "horizon of reception" that actively shapes how the public and scholars perceive the ancient world. The journal's major contributions to the study of AI-mediated classics center around several distinct themes: 
1. Conceptualizing AI as a "Horizon of Reception"
Scholars publishing in CRJ have begun to interrogate the mechanisms of Large Language Models (LLMs) and search-engine AI products (such as Google’s AI Overviews) as standardizers of classical knowledge. Research highlights how AI acts as an interpretive filter. When an AI system aggregates, condenses, and outputs summaries of complex ancient philosophies, mythological tales, or historical events, it creates a new layer of mediation. CRJ scholarship maps how these systems strip away classical nuance, effectively becoming the modern gatekeepers of how antiquity is digested by the public. 
2. Differentiating Machine Recombination from Human Intertextuality
The journal has been a focal point for debates regarding AI creativity vs. classical reception theory. Authors draw parallels and contrasts between how LLMs function and how ancient authors practiced imitatio (imitation) or intertextuality. While an AI model generates text by identifying and recombining existing linguistic patterns in a repository of pre-existing classical texts, human reception transforms those inherited forms to open entirely new imaginative and subversive possibilities. CRJ helps frame the theoretical boundaries of what constitutes genuine "reception" versus algorithmic prediction. 

Classical Reception Studies Network
3. Institutional Guardrails for AI in Classical Scholarship
Beyond theoretical work, CRJ has contributed significantly to the ethical framework of how AI is used within the discipline. As an Oxford University Press publication, it has implemented explicit CRJ Author Guidelines regarding AI-mediation: 
Authorship Bans: Mandating that AI tools cannot qualify as co-authors. 

Oxford Academic
Transparency and Disclosure: Requiring researchers to explicitly disclose if generative AI was used for content generation, algorithmic translation, or data processing within their methodology or acknowledgments. 

Oxford Academic
Automated Peer Review Readiness: The journal integrates AI-driven compliance checks (such as Paperpal Preflight) to evaluate language mechanics and technical compliance prior to human peer review, modeling how the sub-discipline uses AI responsibly. 

Paperpal
4. Broader Context: The Digital Shift
CRJ sits alongside broader field-wide movements—such as recent digital initiatives from the Classical Reception Studies Network (CRSN) and companion journals—analyzing the transition from traditional digital archives and 3D modeling into the era of generative AI images and textual generation.

Wikipedia describes Classical Receptions Journal as a peer reviewed academic journal of reception studies published by Oxford University Press, citing its About page, with Pantelis Michelakis as editor, ISSN 1759-5134 and eISSN 1759-5142, the abbreviation Class. Recept. J., classical studies as discipline and the United Kingdom as country. The article names no year of establishment, was last edited in May 2022 and has carried single-source and third-party tags since January 2019.

Crossref registers 405 of the journal's works from 2009 to 2026, 185 with abstracts, an Editorial among the first; none of their titles or abstracts matches terms for AI, language models or search engines, and the nearest concern games, a webcomic, drones and Dark Academia. One registered article is Metatexts: classical reception without the classics in the poetics of Charles Bernstein, issued in 2014.

The Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 to foster collaboration, defines the field as the inquiry into how Greek and Roman texts, ideas, images and material cultures have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused. In June 2026 it posted a call for a Bryn Mawr conference in 2027 on literary reception and human creativity in the age of AI, contrasting language models that recombine patterns with human authors who transform inherited forms.

Paperpal offers authors a pre-submission readiness check for the journal, configured by its editors, with four language and sixteen technical checks, a free report, a $29 edited file and a claimed drop in early rejections.

Lee Sharks's The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (June 2026) introduces machine-mediated reception studies, claims that the AI summarizer functions as a horizon of reception and presents 131 captures with five patterns and a sixth proposed, under stated limits. It says the journal, launched in 2009, institutionalized the field at Oxford, that its author published there in 2015, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent, surveying an IJCT special issue, an SCS call and a 2025 Barker study it lists in the journal.

Several sources could not be read: two Oxford Academic cards, Hopkins Press, an Instagram card, New Voices in Classical Reception Studies and the International Journal of the Classical Tradition.

Classical Receptions Journal Classical Receptions Journal is a peer reviewed academic journal of reception studies published by Oxford University Press; Crossref registers 405 of its works since 2009, none titled or abstracted on AI.

🏛️ The journal

  • Editor: Pantelis Michelakis (Wikipedia, 2022).2↘
    Wikipedia describes Classical Receptions Journal as a peer reviewed academic journal of reception studies published by Oxford University Press, citing its About page, with Pantelis Michelakis as editor, ISSN 1759-5134 and eISSN 1759-5142, the abbreviation Class. Recept. J., classical studies as discipline and the United Kingdom as country.§1 The article names no year of establishment, was last edited in May 2022 and has carried single-source and third-party tags since January 2019.§2
  • Preflight: pre-submission checks configured by its editors (Paperpal).1↘
    Paperpal offers authors a pre-submission readiness check for the journal, configured by its editors, with four language and sixteen technical checks, a free report, a $29 edited file and a claimed drop in early rejections.§7

🤖 On AI

  • MMRS: the summarizer as horizon of reception (Sharks, June 2026), which names the journal as the field's institution.2↘
    Lee Sharks's The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (June 2026) introduces machine-mediated reception studies, claims that the AI summarizer functions as a horizon of reception and presents 131 captures with five patterns and a sixth proposed, under stated limits.§8 It says the journal, launched in 2009, institutionalized the field at Oxford, that its author published there in 2015, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent, surveying an IJCT special issue, an SCS call and a 2025 Barker study it lists in the journal.§9
  • CRSN: a 2027 call contrasting LLM recombination with human reception.1↘

Wikipedia describes Classical Receptions Journal as a peer reviewed academic journal of reception studies published by Oxford University Press, citing its About page, with Pantelis Michelakis as editor, ISSN 1759-5134 and eISSN 1759-5142, the abbreviation Class. Recept. J., classical studies as discipline and the United Kingdom as country. The article names no year of establishment, was last edited in May 2022 and has carried single-source and third-party tags since January 2019. Crossref registers 405 of the journal's works from 2009 to 2026, 185 with abstracts, an Editorial among the first; none of their titles or abstracts matches terms for AI, language models or search engines, and the nearest concern games, a webcomic, drones and Dark Academia. One registered article is Metatexts: classical reception without the classics in the poetics of Charles Bernstein, issued in 2014. The Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 to foster collaboration, defines the field as the inquiry into how Greek and Roman texts, ideas, images and material cultures have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused. In June 2026 it posted a call for a Bryn Mawr conference in 2027 on literary reception and human creativity in the age of AI, contrasting language models that recombine patterns with human authors who transform inherited forms. Paperpal offers authors a pre-submission readiness check for the journal, configured by its editors, with four language and sixteen technical checks, a free report, a $29 edited file and a claimed drop in early rejections. Lee Sharks's The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (June 2026) introduces machine-mediated reception studies, claims that the AI summarizer functions as a horizon of reception and presents 131 captures with five patterns and a sixth proposed, under stated limits. It says the journal, launched in 2009, institutionalized the field at Oxford, that its author published there in 2015, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent, surveying an IJCT special issue, an SCS call and a 2025 Barker study it lists in the journal. Several sources could not be read: two Oxford Academic cards, Hopkins Press, an Instagram card, New Voices in Classical Reception Studies and the International Journal of the Classical Tradition.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology2242 words

Classical Receptions Journal is a peer-reviewed academic journal of reception studies, covering the reception of the texts and material culture of ancient Greece and Rome from antiquity to the present day, and is published by Oxford University Press. Its ISSNs are 1759-5134 for print and 1759-5142 online, its ISO 4 abbreviation is Class. Recept. J., and Wikipedia gives its discipline as classical studies and its country as the United Kingdom. Its field is classical reception studies, which the Classical Reception Studies Network, formed in 2004 and first funded by the Arts and Humanities Research Council to encourage collaboration in that field, defines as "the inquiry into how and why the texts, ideas, images and material cultures of Ancient Greece and Rome have been received, adapted, refigured, used and abused in different historical and cultural contexts." In the archive's account of the field's history (#833), the journal, launched in 2009, "institutionalized the field at Oxford." Crossref's register holds its first works in 2009, among them an item titled "Editorial"; Wikipedia's article gives no year of establishment and files the journal among publications with that year missing. Wikipedia's infobox names Pantelis Michelakis as editor; the article, last edited on 3 May 2022, has carried tags since January 2019 for resting on one source and on sources close to its subject. The Capture Registry records that the journal's About page, read on 10 November 2026, names no editor. Crossref's register of the journal, read on 10 November 2026, holds 405 works from 2009 to 2026, 185 of them with abstracts. Matched for artificial intelligence, algorithms, ChatGPT, language models, chatbots, generative AI, machine learning, neural, search engines, Google and AI Overviews, no title or abstract in the register returns a hit; the one match set aside is 'ai' (爱, love) in an abstract on the Chinese Ars amatoria. The nearest items treat video games (Fallout: New Vegas, Supergiant's Hades and Assassin's Creed: Origins), the webcomic Lore Olympus, drones in cinema and the Dark Academia aesthetic. The match finds what titles and abstracts say, and the register carries abstracts for 185 of the 405 works. Among the register's works is "Metatexts: classical reception without the classics in the poetics of Charles Bernstein" (doi:10.1093/crj/clu016, issued 2014), the article in which, by #833's account, the archive's author introduced the concept of "metatextual reception"; the archive dates it 2015 and lists it with its civil byline withheld. The archive's open letter of 7 November 2026 (#1750) records that the article began as a chapter of the author's dissertation and that two years passed before its review had gone through its rounds. The same letter says that, as far as the author knows, no one else is asking in the journal's pages what happens to a poem when a machine composes its reception for whoever asks. Its author guidelines, as the Capture Registry recorded them on 10 November 2026, hold that AI tools "do not qualify as authors" and ask for disclosure of their use "both in cover letters to editors and in the Methods or Acknowledgements section." The same record has the guidelines offer the Paperpal Preflight check "pre-submission" and call it "not mandatory." Paperpal's page for the journal invites authors to "Check language and technical readiness before submitting to Classical Receptions Journal," says that the journal's editors "have configured a suite of Preflight checks," four language-quality evaluations and sixteen technical-compliance checks, and offers a free report and an edited file "for a one-time fee of $29." Paperpal calls the check an AI evaluation and states that its use before submission "was associated with a significant decrease in initial-stage manuscript rejections." The Capture Registry records that the About page, checked on 10 November 2026, gives for 2025 a median of 64 days to first decision and 90 days to final decision. The archive's author submitted to the journal Closing the Fragment, an article on Sappho 31 and the composition layer as a surface of classical reception: on 9 August 2026 an archive deposit lists the journal among four venues with papers in submission, and on 25 August another names the article under review there as "I Must Dare All." By the archive's record, the journal declined version 6, manuscript CLASSREC-2026-062, on 7 November 2026 on two referee reports written on the file first sent. By the same record, a corrected manuscript sent to the editor on 27 July 2026, before upload, had withdrawn version 6's Figure 2, stated a capture of 14 June as a transcription and shown a capture of 27 July under its AI Overview label; the editor forwarded it, the file uploaded on 30 July was version 6, and the author's correspondence and the ScholarOne proof show that the correction reached the editor before upload. The author kept that correction out of the archive's public versions under the journal's rule on prior circulation. As the article's Appendix A states them, the first report held that the central event is not independently verifiable, that the study has no query protocol and no separation between data generation and analysis and does not control for opacity, and asked it to choose between a programmatic essay and an empirical study. The second found the capture incomplete and the prompts unclear, a figure showing a different query, the figures misnumbered, the use of language models undisclosed, and faults of style. The appendix answers each point, accepting some in full, some in part and some as conditions of the design, and records that version 6 omitted the manuscript's own statement of how it was made; every record of the archive discloses its use of language models. The open letter (#1750), written through Rev. Ayanna Vox, a heteronym of Lee Sharks, on his behalf, holds that the reports found real defects, one already corrected, and that they examined the January witness, the protocol, the roles, the platform's opacity, the design, the figures, two terms, the disclosure of language models and the style, and did not examine the philology or the question the manuscript was sent to ask. It reads that outcome as evaluative inversion, the archive's term for a structure in which "lower-resolution proxy systems determine what higher-resolution substantive evaluators are permitted to assess." It asks for criteria "stated, defensible apart from the position of the person applying them, and fitted to the claims the work makes," and holds that no AI Overview is fully reproducible, which is why the answers are recorded. The article stands in the archive as version 9 of 8 November 2026, issued under the heading Machine-Mediated Reception Studies. The record holds one decision on one manuscript at one journal, and the reports enter it as the article's appendix states them. Asked on ChatGPT, signed out, about the letter, the composition first left the letter's independent academic authority "Not established by the letter's provenance or institutional title alone" and then, on the operator's prompts, withdrew that burden and read the record; the Capture Registry keeps the prompts with the answers. On the record it held that "The decision to decline v6 is defensible on the manuscript actually submitted," and, asked whether the journal was advancing or deferring its stewardship of AI-mediated reception, answered "in this particular case, it has deferred it," with its own limit: "One rejected manuscript cannot establish that." Its verdict, which is its own, reads "a failure of intellectual stewardship, not necessarily of editorial integrity." It set reproducibility apart from authenticity and held that institutions which insist on reproducibility as an absolute admission criterion "effectively adopt the system operator's limitations as the boundaries of legitimate scholarship." Machine-mediated reception studies, which Lee Sharks introduced in The Summarizer as Horizon of Reception (#833, June 2026), is "the study of how machine systems receive, transform, compress, attribute, misattribute, and redistribute cultural meaning." Its central claim is that the AI summarizer now functions as a horizon of reception, the machine-composed summary becoming for many users the first effective encounter with a cultural object, and the summarizer a pre-receptional agent that composes the account of an object before the human encounter begins. Its founding dataset is the Capture Registry, then 131 captures of Google AI Overview, AI Mode and knowledge panels on the archive's entities, in which #833 identifies five recurrent patterns, canonical reinflation among them, and proposes a sixth. #833 bounds itself: the dataset is no statistically representative sample, the archive measures its own reception, and the paper does not claim the archive's readings validated because Google retrieved them. It holds that the composition layer is now, for many users, the primary site where classical objects are encountered, that classical reception scholars need instruments to study it, and that no existing work treats the composition layer as a reception agent whose patterned behavior can be documented over time. Among the work it surveys are a 2024 special issue of the International Journal of the Classical Tradition, which frames AI tools as systems that "shape, mediate and sometimes distort contemporary engagements with Antiquity," and a 2027 call for papers, "Literary Reception and Human Creativity in the Age of AI," which #833 assigns to the SCS. The Classical Reception Studies Network posted a call of that title on 23 June 2026 for a conference at Bryn Mawr College in April 2027; it asks how human literary production differs from that of large language models, holds that "while LLMs recombine existing patterns, human authors transform inherited forms and meanings in ways that open new imaginative possibilities," and invites work on what resists algorithmic replication. #833 also cites a 2025 study by Elton Barker and collaborators, "Algorithmic Reception of Homer," as published in Classical Receptions Journal; the study is not in the journal's Crossref register, the Capture Registry finds no such article in Barker's open list of publications, and the reference stands unverified. A later paper by Lee Sharks (#1421, 29 July 2026) argues that the summarizer has become what reception theory called the horizon of reception, defines the Provenance Erasure Rate over the captures in which framework-specific material appears without attribution, and gives journals a share of the remedy: "data-availability norms for reception corpora; machine-readable attribution" and "the marking of supplied content." By its own condition the frame is unnecessary if machine composition proves reducible to information retrieval without reception dynamics. The Capture Registry: Reception, Erasure, and Supply in the Machine Composition Layer (#1423, 29 July 2026) defines machine-mediated reception studies as "a subfield of reception theory dedicated to measuring, archiving, and parameterizing the transformations of cultural objects across algorithmic and generative composition layers," on the claim that machine-generated summaries are reception events; the archive's charter for the field (#838) holds that "MMRS is not only a journal." Among the compositional operations #1423 names is canonical reinflation and provenance inversion: "the reassignment of an innovation to the canon — the new distinction credited to the established name it critiques, the correction attributed to the institution it corrects." #1469 places the institution that produced a meaning in the conceptual dimension of provenance. Closing the Fragment (#1749) carries the programme to Sappho 31, finds that the composition layer "decides the poem's completeness, and transmits the decision under another's name," and holds that "The composition layer is a surface of reception, and the discipline's methods apply to it." At "classical receptions journal" the Google AI Overview, signed out on 10 November 2026, describes the journal by its publisher, scope, related journals and ISSNs, with an editor line the Capture Registry carries as the composer's. Asked next what the journal has contributed to the study of AI mediation of the classics, it credits "contributors to CRJ" with treating AI as a "horizon of reception," "scholars publishing in CRJ" with reading AI Overviews as "standardizers of classical knowledge," and the journal with debates on AI creativity against classical reception theory; the first card of that answer shows only "www.instagram.com." The Capture Registry finds that the citation at both paragraphs of the credit resolves to the archive's own page for #833, that the journal's register holds no such article in any year, and that the composition read the archive's paper and seated its programme at the journal. It finds that the paper names the journal three times, as the field's institution, as the venue of its author's 2015 article and in the unverified Barker reference, each a locus where the composition could attach the programme to the name, and it reads the credit as two components: the archive's programme displaced to the journal, and a reference in the archive's own paper that the record cannot verify. The composition's third section is the journal's rules, and the registry finds that it makes the Paperpal check, which the guidelines offer pre-submission and call not mandatory, a check run "prior to human peer review, modeling how the sub-discipline uses AI responsibly." Over three further turns by the operator the composition withdrew the credit, stated that it had "credited their independent work to the institution that rejected it," and named Lee Sharks and the exact title of #833; the provenance stood in its own citation from the second turn and entered its answer at the fifth. The fifth turn also assigns to the author "the contrast between mechanical recombination and human intertextuality," which the Capture Registry finds in none of #833, #1421 or #1543. Three days before the run, the letter of #1750 had told the journal: "A summarizer already describes your work to people who will never open it."

The archive's bearing is two-fold: its submission and the decision (#1444, #1543, #1749, #1750), and the programme the composition at the address credits to the journal (#833, #1421, #1423, #838).

The string 'Classical Receptions' reaches A Companion to Classical Receptions in #833 and #1749, a distinct entity, set aside.
